paragraphs: Among the proofs that visual perception (ruʾyat al-baṣar) cannot apply to God (mighty and exalted): every proof that has been adduced for the liceity of visual perception of God can be paralleled by a proof for the liceity of tactile perception of God. For if someone argues: every self-subsistent thing, when it comes close to me, when the light connects me to it, and when the veils and obstacles are removed, I see it with my eye — well, by the same form: every self-subsistent thing, when it comes close to me, and when the obstacles and veils are removed, I touch it with my hand. So every proof for the licit-ness of ruʾya of God commits the proponent to the same liceity for touch — and this is absurd. The visible-by-sight must, of necessity, face the eye, with a distance between them; if that holds, then God is in a place rather than another place; He is in front of me, not behind; He becomes near me, then nearer, until I touch Him. All of this is plain kufr.[{2}]

If they say: but you allow that we see colors and motions without the colors and motions being themselves bodies — we reply: it is not our doctrine that we see the color alone without the colored thing, or the motion alone without the moving thing. Whoever licenses the visual perception of an accident (color, motion) is also committed to the tactile perception of an accident (heat, cold, roughness). For when one judges a body to be rough, one judges by placing the hand on it; one must then say that the touch has perceived the roughness as such. Similarly: when we see a moving body with our eyes, we know its motion via sight, and distinguish it from a resting body by sight, having seen both its motion and its rest. And every visible-by-sight, if a dense body, conceals what is behind it. [The argument continues — partly defective at Cairo l. 5398. The recoverable sense: if you grant that bodies are seen, and that motions and colors are seen as properties-of-bodies, you have no grounds to grant visibility to what is not a body in any sense at all. God, not being a body, cannot be the object of any of the sensory faculties — neither sight nor touch nor any other.] ---
